claims.text: Configurational entropy predominantly governs elevated-temperature structural and chemical stability in near-equimolar high-entropy nanoalloys.
High configurational entropy suppresses large-scale phase separation.
Strong local enthalpic interactions can produce partial short-range order despite configurational-entropy stabilization.
The proposed specimens are nanocrystalline, near-equimolar powders containing three to five principal elements, consolidated and moderately homogenized.
The specimens will be heated incrementally to about 1200 °C while phase evolution and local ordering are monitored by in-situ XRD and TEM.
Heating will occur in inert gas or vacuum at approximately 10 °C per minute with measurements at temperature holds.
Short-range chemical ordering or clustering can offset configurational-entropy stabilization.
Increasing temperature strengthens the configurational-entropy contribution favoring a single-phase solid solution.
Local chemical interactions may drive clustering or ordering and create short-range compositional inhomogeneities.
Local clustering or ordering can either assist or limit complete phase stabilization.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will remain mostly single-phase to higher temperatures than a conventional multiphase alloy lacking comparable configurational disorder.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will form fewer or smaller secondary phases than the baseline alloy.
Short-range ordering will produce detectable peak-broadening or diffuse-scattering signatures.
Local ordering can occur without extensive macroscopic segregation.
A lower-configurational-entropy baseline alloy will develop secondary phases and chemical segregation earlier or more extensively under identical thermal cycles.
The prediction applies when mixing entropy is sufficiently large to delay or suppress phase separation.
The prediction is restricted to systems having moderate atomic-size and chemical-potential differences.
Strongly exothermic interactions or large atomic-size mismatch may cause deviation from entropy-dominated stability.
Systematically changing composition to alter mixing enthalpy can test whether entropy or local enthalpic interactions dominate phase stability.

Repeated significant multiphase formation or rapid segregation below the predicted stability temperatures across multiple nominally entropy-stabilized compositions would falsify configurational entropy as the primary governing factor.
